articleTitle: Standard frequency and time signal transmissions from the union observatory, Johannesburg
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: Deviations of frequencies and time signals are with respect to the weighted mean of six quartz oscillators, and time signals from WWV over 20-day intervals. A positive frequency deviation indicates that the frequency was high. A time deviation of 010 indicates that the time pulses were 0.010 second late on WWV while 990 indicates that they were 0.010 second early. A value of 46.3 milliseconds has been adopted for the propagation time of radio signals between Washington and Johannesburg.

articleTitle: Author's reply to discussion
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: Mr Lindley (in reply): I would like to thank Mr Bishop for his comments on the paper and for raising a number of interesting points. The ‘pebble-bed’ reactor is quite a fascinating theoretical concept but in my view suffers from a number or fundamental technical objections. To be economic a power plant must have an acceptable first cost, a satisfactory efficiency, moderate maintenance costs, and a high ‘availability’ (i.e. out of action only for maintenance, etc., for short periods of time in total per annum). If any of these four criteria is grossly violated then the system proposed is most unlikely to be satisfactory for electric power generation. With a plant of high capital cost it is particularly important that the availability should be high and maintenance costs low. The ‘pebble-bed’ plant with its highly radioactive coolant circuit, boilers, etc., will, I feel sure, show a disappointingly low availability and high maintenance costs. In addition to these problems there are a large number of technical difficulties in the design and control of the reactor which remain to be resolved.

abstract: Mr Basson has raised a very important point. The complex control systems envisaged in the paper must be very reliable otherwise the delays they cause will more than outweigh the advantages they introduce. To ensure a high degree of reliability and to minimize any downtimes, the availability of good maintenance and operating instructions is essential. Every effort is made to use equipment and schemes which are simple and reliable but nothing is 100 per cent reliable and the more components that there are the more likely it is statistically that there will be a failure. Therefore, the maintenance personnel must be trained and given every facility for instruction. In this direction we agree entirely with the idea of showing the actual build-up and principles employed by the designer in constructing the scheme. Short notes with skeleton diagrams can augment the normal instruction manuals.

articleTitle: Author's reply to discussion
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: Dr Hewitt asks whether my Company has published any independent data on the values of various types of terrain for producing a back scatter signal, but, as far as I know, they have not. Investigation of this phenomenon has been carried out for a long time and 1 think it is fair to say that investigation of back scatter on microwaves has been going on since the days of the H2S, which was about the earliest of the vertical incidence radar scanners used on aircraft. Since that time there has been quite a lot of work done, much of it by Government Departments or by firms under Government development contracts, and there have not been very many papers published. Of the papers used by my own organization, the first was produced by Wiltshire, Schlesinger and Johnson entitled “Backscattering Characteristics of the Sea” in the region of 10 to 15 000 megacycles”, that is to say from 2 cm to 30 metres. This was published in the “Proceedings of the I.R.E.”, an American Journal, in February 1957. A second paper was published in July, 1959, by Grant and Yattley on “Backscattering from water and land, centrimetric and milimetric wavelengths”, also in the Proceedings of the I.R.E., July, 1957, and J.P. Campbell also produced a paper on the same subject, April, 1958, which was published by the American Civil Aviation Aeronautical Organization, in April, 1958.

abstract: In reply to Dr Thompson, we can say that the practice of our firm has been to connect cells in series and parallel without other means of ensuring load and voltage sharing and to rate the cells accordingly. It is conceivable that under some conditions additional steps to ensure sharing may become justified but our present view is that simple series and parallel connection has much to recommend it. articleTitle: Electrical control systems in heavy industry (particularly in Steel mills)
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: The paper begins by defining the basic objects underlying control system design. The historical background is covered briefly and this leads on to the principles of feedback control system design. A description is given of the types of power sources, components and control schemes found in heavy industry, reference being made to the means of attaining the required performance. Both static and rotary equipment are considered. The fundamental chain of command and control is then described this being linked to the theme of fundamental control and the developments of the present and not too far distant future where the operator is moved further and further back in the control chain. This covers the storage, sequencing and measuring equipment which is used for this purpose. The authors conclude that the trend towards completely controlled processes will continue. Systems will be developed which are sufficiently reliable and economic but their adoption will depend to a large extent on the close co-operation of designer and user.

publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: It is customary for the Presidential Address to be related to the President's life's work. While considering the possible subjects for this address, I thought it probable that as it is the Institute's fiftieth birthday this year, many of you would find a review of the early history of the Institute and the progress in electrical engineering in the last fifty years of interest. This address will broadly cover this period.

articleTitle: Fission and fusion: The ninth bernard price memorial lecture
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: To be invited to give the Bernard Price Memorial lecture on the occasion of your Golden Jubilee is indeed a signal honour for which I am most grateful. In coming here I too can pay my respects to a great engineer and benefactor to science. I recall showing Bernard Price some artificial lightning discharges of one to three million volts in the High Voltage Laboratory of the Metropolitan-Vickers Electrical Company and describing to him how our studies of the spark discharge had been of direct help to Dr Schonland in developing ideas of the mechanism of the lightning discharge. His visit occurred at the time when he must have been contemplating the creation of the Geophysical Institute here, and I collaborated in further research with Dr Schonland after he became director of the Institute, so I feel my links with Bernard Price are fairly strong.

articleTitle: High frequency transistor parameters and their experimental determination
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: For the specialized application of transistors, some knowledge of their electrical and physical characteristics is required. As is the case with valves, transistor manufacturers supply a limited amount of data about their product to serve as a guide for the design engineer. However, with the transistor art at its present state of development, there still exists some controversy about what the most relevant data is that has to accompany the device into the hands of the experimenter.

articleTitle: The development of register-translators for use in large automatic telephone networks
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: The development of telephone systems throughout the last half-century has been noticeable for the increasing automatization of calls. At the beginning of the period all but a few local calls were made via one or more operators; at the end of the period some subscribers are able to complete almost every call automatically and only a small proportion of calls require more than one operator. This development is common to all the countries of the world though it has, of course, progressed to varying lengths.

articleTitle: The theory and practice of electronic testing of winding ropes
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: Over the past few years, the South African mining industry has been actively furthering the use of electronic rope testing equipment based on the type described in previous papers. The results have continued to be promising and the number of ropes which are tested on a routine basis, with both the prototype and the new improved types of equipment, are continually increasing. At the time of writing, more than 500 ropes over one inch in diameter are regularly examined with electronic equipment every four months. With information coming in at this rate, it is not surprising that a considerable amount of experience has been obtained in a short time.

articleTitle: The engineer's place in the modern corporate enterprise
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: I am indeed grateful to your President and to the officers and members of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers for the honour of being asked to participate in your Golden Jubilee. This important event is deeply significant as a manifestation of your dedication to the improvement of the engineering profession. In terms of this endless task which your Institute has undertaken with such imagination, there is no magic in the number 50, but it is clear that your Golden Jubilee has for its purpose not merely the celebration of the passage of time. You are by the very comprehensiveness of this series of meetings, not only inventorying technical developments which are significant in a material sense, but much more important, you are taking stock of our profession to examine critically what and how we can contribute to the enhancement of the economic well-being of the society in which we live.

articleTitle: D. C. drives for winders
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: It is generally accepted that the type of control obtainable with the Ward-Leonard drive is the most suitable for mine winder operation and all developments on other electrical drives for winder have striven to achieve a similar control. There are, however, a number of other factors which affect the decision on the type of drive to use on any particular installation. The most important of these, viz power consumption, voltage regulation, maximum demand, capital cost, heat dissipation and harmonics, are considered in the paper and a comparison is made between Ward-Leonard, rectifier and a.c. drives in relation to these factors. For many years, open-loop control of winders has provided adequate control characteristics but the more stringent operational requirements for modern electric winders have resulted in the development of closed-loop control systems. Two such systems, one for a Ward-Leonard drive and the other for a rectifier drive, are described and the arrangements for obtaining automatic retardation of the winder as the conveyances approach the terminal points of the shaft are discussed. Operational results obtained on winders employing these systems arc given and attention is given to the means for stopping the winder in emergencies. It is concluded that the results obtained with the closed loop Ward-Leonard system are sufficiently accurate to meet present requirements but that some improvement is still desirable on the rectifier winder. Future developments would, therefore, appear to be aimed mainly at the application of new techniques to achieve similar results.

abstract: M. J. Grindrod (Associate Member, 1938) died in Durban on 7th March 1959. Mr Grindrod joined the Victoria Falls and Transvaal Power Co. Ltd. (the predecessor to Escom's Rand Undertaking) in 1926. At an early stage of his career with the V.F.P. he was appointed to a position in the Control Department, eventually becoming Assistant Senior Control Engineer. He transferred to the Natal Undertakings of Escom in 1954 and worked on the Engineering Staff in the Durban Offices until his untimely death. He is survived by his widow and three children.

articleTitle: Obituary: Leonard Hulford Loder Badham
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: It is with deep regret that Council records the death of Leonard Hulford Loder Badham (Past President, Honorary Member) who died suddenly on the 3rd August, 1959, while on holiday at Sani Pass Hotel, Natal. About four years ago his health caused considerable anxiety but, with characteristic courage, he overcame one setback after another until eventually he was able to resume his work and other interests through which he had become known to so many in engineering and industrial spheres in the Union. Consequently, his sudden and unexpected death came as a great shock to his many friends and colleagues.
